extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and scholarly-communication stakeholders interested in peer review practice and innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply criteria for assessing peer review systems and practices (including openness, transparency, role distinctions, platform effects, reviewer recognition, and quality-control basics) in scholarly publishing. Focus is on innovations and future directions for peer review of scientific papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of peer review: gate-keeping vs improving manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-review functions both as a gate-keeper (deciding acceptance/rejection) and as a means to improve manuscript quality (formative/developmental role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors and commenters note the paper emphasises gate-keeping but pays little attention to peer review's formative role. Reviewers/authors can engage in interactive review to improve manuscripts; Scott Armstrong recommends referees only comment (not recommend acceptance/rejection) and leave decisions to editors as a way to encourage innovation and constructive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive / collaborative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of interactive review where reviewers and authors work together to reach a final draft (collaborative peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called out as an important means for improving manuscripts; Frontiers' interactive review model is cited as an innovation that facilitates this. The paper mentions interactive review (Table 2) but does not discuss it in depth — reviewers recommend expanding on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms as enablers or obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of technology platforms can either enable or obstruct innovative forms of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good and bad platforms are 'vital enablers for/obstacles' to innovation. The paper is critiqued for spending space on platforms with little impact and neglecting established platforms (including the authors' own). Consider platform maturity and actual impact when assessing innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish major-impact innovations from small-scale experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a clear distinction between innovations that have already had a major impact (e.g., the advent of preprint servers) and many small-scale experiments that have not had such impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate space and weight in analyses according to demonstrated impact. The reviewer recommends separating widely-adopted innovations from local/experimental efforts to avoid misleading emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish peer review from reader commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate traditional peer review (as academics understand it) from reader commentary; peer review is typically evaluative and plays a vital role, while reader commentary has been marginal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confounding the two can distract from the main theme; the paper should clearly separate mechanisms that serve formal scholarly validation from post-publication commentary systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope fidelity: focus on peer review of scientific papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep discussion focused on peer review of scientific papers and avoid digressions into peer review in other areas (e.g., software) unless directly relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers/reviewers cautioned that examples from other fields, while interesting, can distract from the central topic and should be minimized or explicitly connected to the main theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness components: availability of reviews vs reviewer identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review (OPR) involves multiple criteria such as making reviews available and revealing reviewer identity; availability of reviews may be more important than identity for verifying review occurred and advancing knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter suggests the order of importance in the paper's OPR criteria should be reversed: availability of reviews first, reviewer identity second. Consider which openness dimensions most directly support transparency and scholarly value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency metrics (PRE example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency of the peer review process should include explicit metadata such as peer review method, number of rounds of review, and number of reviewers and editors involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer Review Evaluation (PRE) (AAAS) provides a tangible example: a visible seal that, when clicked, pops up details about review method and rounds. Such signals increase transparency even when full open peer review is not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and standardized descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize the description of peer review activities to make them easier to describe, attribute, recognize and reward (e.g., Publons, Academic Karma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to standardize metadata/description (not necessarily the activity itself) so peer review work can be recognized and rewarded. Decoupled services and aggregators can help capture review contributions for credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-control basics to check during editorial processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals' QC processes should check basics such as presence of ethics statements, trial registration, and the use of reporting guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QC includes initial checks (ethics/trial registration/reporting guidelines) through to in-depth methodological review. Emphasise these basics as core functions of journal processes to help ensure reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility as a core objective of QC and peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: One core role of journals' QC and peer review is to attempt to ensure reproducibility of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and journal processes are components aiming to improve reproducibility. As other publication types (preprints) grow, QC basics will become more critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and conduct in commenting systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of problems associated with commenting platforms—especially tone—and the risks posed by anonymous or pseudonymous sites (e.g., PubPeer, Reddit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity can produce tone problems; the paper is critiqued for not discussing these sufficiently. Moderation, community norms, and platform design are relevant evaluative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of substantive post-publication review (e.g., Twitter debates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review can occur outside formal systems (e.g., Twitter) and sometimes constitutes substantial peer review; such occurrences should be acknowledged and discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers noted notable cases where substantive critique and review began in social media, and recommend discussing such phenomena and their implications for formal peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency in meta/review articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Review articles or literature reviews should describe their methodology: databases searched, keywords used, inclusion/exclusion criteria, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewer recommended the paper strengthen its review portion by stating the search methodology; systematic description improves credibility and reproducibility of the review itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting and archiving practices to preserve evidence (link rot prevention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use web archiving tools (Wayback Machine, WebCite, Perma.cc) and recommended DOI formatting (https://doi.org rather than http://dx.doi.org) to ensure longevity and correctness of web references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent link rot and ensure longevity of evidence cited in articles, journals should require or encourage web archiving for non-DOI links and follow CrossRef recommendations for DOI formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward mechanisms for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may reward reviewers via free subscriptions, APC discounts (including OA journals), or payment (notably for some types like statistical reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different journals and models offer various incentives; these practical rewards are part of the ecosystem to recognize peer review labor and may be evaluated when considering review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests and affiliation transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers should transparently declare competing interests and affiliations (e.g., declare relationships with commercial platforms mentioned in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comments dispute adequacy of competing interest statements; clear, explicit declaration of relevant affiliations is required to avoid perceived conflicts (e.g., mentioning employer, funding of APCs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative characterisation of (some) pre-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: As presented in Table 2, some assessments categorise pre-publication peer review as 'Non-transparent, impossible to evaluate, biased, secretive, exclusive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing highlights potential failure modes of opaque traditional peer review; reviewers caution about emotive language and advise balancing critique with nuance and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility vs publisher responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors manage editorial/review processes while publishers handle business processes; responsibility for peer review design and management lies primarily with editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction matters when assessing who should implement changes or bear accountability; conflating editors and publishers can misattribute control over peer review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial expertise: editors are often peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors themselves are frequently acknowledged experts and peers; the distinction between editors and peer reviewers can be false with regard to expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating processes, consider that editor decisions often rely on editors' scholarly expertise as much as external reviewers; this affects assessments of review quality and roles.
